Death In China

By: Sibusisiwe Buthelezi | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What happens when a South African citizen dies while working abroad.

Unique Selling Point:
We speak to someone who has been tasked with bringing back bodies of South African teachers who die abroad, her methods, unconventional to say the least.

Summary:
In August last year, 26-year-old Jarred Anthony Clegg left South Africa for China, where he would be teaching. It was an exciting time for both he and his family as teaching was his passion. Jarred had gotten hold of the opportunity through an agent that had previously sent many South African teachers to China. All was well until June this year.

Four months ago, Noeleen Venter, Jarred's mom, received a call from someone who identified themselves as Jarred's friend and colleague who was also based in China. The caller told Noeleen that Jarred had died and the family needed to make arrangements to bring his body back to SA. Noeleen then contacted the agency Jarred was employed by and they confirmed his death, stating that he had died naturally in his apartment. However soon after, Noeleen received a document stating that Jarred had died in an accident and had been convicted of manslaughter. While she was processing this information, she received a document stating that Jarred had died under suspicious circumstances and the matter was now handed to the police for a criminal investigation. Lastly, she was told that her son was a victim of an accident where a vehicle had crashed into him and he died. Sitting with four official documents stating different causes of death, she reached out to a lawyer.

Months later, she is desperate to get her son's ashes back but is now receicving a cold shoulder from Dirco, the Chinese Embassy as well as the agent that Jarred was employed by. All Noeleen wants is to know what happened to her son and just where are his ashes.

In an effort to get more information, researchg has led us to Nadia who is a South African teacher based in China. She explained that many families find themselves in the same position as Noeleen. She says on many occassions, she has had to carry ashes of deceased South Africans in her luggage during her visits back to South Africa. She says they do this in order to cut costs of transporting the back to SA.

We've also gotten hold of an agency that is based in Pretoria, they help place teachers in China and help them get their paperwork processed. The agency says they constantly have issues with DIRCO and the SA consulate in China not playing ball in cases where there are issues or even deaths of SA citizens in China.

Press Release:


Death in China
Jarred Clegg was just 26 years old when he moved to China to fulfil his dream of teaching English. Just months later, his mother received a devastating call: Jarred had died overseas. But even as she struggled to process her loss, she was baffled by conflicting accounts of his death. Was it natural – suspicious – or tragic accident? Meanwhile, authorities turned a cold shoulder to pleas for assistance in repatriating Jarred’s body. What happens when a South African citizen dies working abroad? It’s the story of a mysterious death, bureaucratic blunders, an unconventional solution – and most of all, a mother desperate for closure.
Producer: Sebe Buthelezi | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


(MacFarlane)- It was a move promising to change lives.
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- She was educated and then we thought she would break the
(Noeleen Venter)- He was very excited about it because it was like three times
as much as what he was earning.
(MacFarlane)- Teaching English abroad, a growing trend among our youth.
(MacFarlane)- But what happens when those young people die under uncertain circumstances? How do grieving families piece together the final moments of their loves ones?
(Clayson Monyela)- China is a sovereign country, South Africa has no legal right to send a team to go and investigate something like this.
(MacFarlane)- And how do they get their bodies home?
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- The first company, they told us they will bring her body for R300 thousand. The other one was R400 thousand.
(MacFarlane)- Families are left, desperate for answers.
(MacFarlane)- With the youth unemployment rate sitting at just over 45% in this country, to escape becoming a statistic, many are flocking to China, to go and teach English.
(AI Voice)- Ready for an adventure? Teaching English in China is more than just a job, it’s a journey. You’ll inspire young minds, discover a rich culture, taste incredible food and explore landmarks thousands of years old.
(MacFarlane)- The jobs offer potential salaries of between R20 000 and close to R90 thousand a month.
(MacFarlane)- It was an offer too enticing to miss for 26-year-old Jarred Clegg.
(Noeleen Venter)- He was in Kimberely first and he taught there, then he got a job in Libya for eight months.
(Noeleen Venter)- While he was there, he got this job in China.
(MacFarlane)- His mother, Noeleen Venter, lives in George in the Western Cape. She says Jarred moved to China to teach English in August last year.
(Noeleen Venter)- He used to love children, Jarred used to absolutely love
children.
(McFarlane)- You can’t be a teacher if you don’t love kids right.
(Noeleen Venter)- No. He was very happy in his working environment, from what I picked up.
(McFarlane)- But in June this year, Jarred’s updates suddenly stopped.
(Noeleen Venter)- We were worried because we hadn’t heard from him for a few days.
(McFarlane)- She contacted the travel agent Jarred had used to process his
paperwork.
(McFarlane)- In turn, the agent, Hitekani Maluleke, contacted Jarred’s employer.
(Hitekani Maluleke)- He said, “I reported him to the consulate in Shangai”. I thought maybe he did something wrong and I asked what did you report him for? And then he said, “He died”.
(McFarlane)- Before she could deliver the news, Noeleen received a call from the South African consulate.
(Noeleen Venter)- It’s like.. I can’t explain the emotions, it’s like something hits you.. it’s like a ten ton boulder hitting you.
(Noeleen Venter)- They only told me that they found him in his bedroom, they never told me how or anything about how he died or anything.
(McFarlane)- But Noeleen grew suspicious after receiving conflicting police reports on Jarred’s death.
(McFarlane)- This after she filed a claim with his travel insurer.
(Noeleen Venter)- The insurance company said he died of an illness, then I asked them for the proof, so they sent me a police report which said he was convicted of manslaughter and another one said he was negligently killed.
(Noeleen Venter)- The big thing is I want answers. I want to know if he suffered, I want to know those things.
(McFarlane)- Wanting to get to the truth, she called for her son’s body to be returned home.
(McFarlane)- But she was quoted half a million rand.
(McFarlane)- This wasn’t the first time a South African had died while working as a teacher in China.

(McFarlane)- In April 2022, Nomaqocwa Blackie, was found dead in her Shangai apartment. The cause of death, unknown.
(McFarlane)- It took nearly three months for her body to return home.
(McFarlane)- Five months later, a woman called Lusanda Sixaxeni, passed away from an unknown illness.
(McFarlane)- Through public donations, her family managed to raise the R400 000 required to bring her home, more than a month after her passing.
(McFarlane)- For Siphosethu Mqokozo’s family, the story had a different ending
(McFarlane)- Nolubabalo Mqokozo, vividly recalls the excitement as her sister moved to China in 2019.
(McFarlane)- The youngest of five children, and the only one with a degree, the family were pinning their hopes on Sethu, as they affectionately called her.
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- We were happy because we thought we have someone who is working abroad and everything will be fine.
(MacFarlane)- Did she tell you why she chose China?
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- Because she didn’t get a job here, she did apply many times but she didn’t get anything.
(MacFarlane)- But in September 2022, the family received tragic news from someone identifying himself as Sethu’s friend.
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- He called us and told us Sethu passed on and then he gave me a number to call. They told me it’s a panic attack.
(MacFarlane)- Panic attack?
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- Yes.
(MacFarlane)- Nolubabalo contacted the school Sethu worked for to try and retrace her final moments
(MacFarlane)- Management claimed she had called in sick on the day in question and later took herself to a local clinic.
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- When she got there they said she was getting worse then they took her in an ambulance and then she passed on, on her way to hospital.
(MacFarlane)- What happens when a loved one dies abroad, and then travel insurance rejects the claim?
(MacFarlane)- This is a position that many South African families find themselves in.
(Clayson Monyela)- There is no government that will ever have a budget enough to pay, to repatriate the mortal remains of nationals who pass on in foreign countries. There’s no government that does that.
(MacFarlane)- Deputy Director General at the Department of International Relations, Clayson Monyela, says there’s only so much they can provide.
(MacFarlane)- A lot of families have come out obviously against the department, saying that they don’t feel they’re getting the support. They’ve been quite critical of the department as a result of this.
(Clayson Monyela)- I guess the issue is really continuing with the awareness campaigns so that there is no expectation from families that when something like this happens, government will pay because government is simply not able to do that.
(MacFarlane)- We questioned him on Dirco’s alleged failures to communicate with Noeleen.
(Clayson Monyela)- In this particular case, I checked the records. Our team both here and in China did what was necessary and was correct and were very responsive.
(MacFarlane)- Monyela says the only solution is to take up travel insurance.
(Hitekani Maluleke)- Most of the expats are leaving for a longer period of time, the longest insurance that I have seen, that actually covers repatriation has been 90 days.
(MacFarlane)- For five months, Nolubabalo and her family hosted fundraising events to bring Sethu’s remains home, after the insurer claimed Sethu’s cover had expired.
(MacFarlane)- In the end, they were backed into a corner.
(Mqokozo family)- Businesses or anyone who can donate, please help so that her remains can be returned back here to Malahleni.
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- We couldn’t bring her body so we decided to cremate it.
(MacFarlane)- Was it a difficult decision to make because those aren’t things that we do as Africans, we don’t cremate.
(Nolubabalo Mqokozo)- Yes. Because even the parents said, “No we can’t do that, we’ve never seen a cremation. We want the body”.
(MacFarlane)- For citizens who die abroad, cremation is the cheaper alternative.
(MacFarlane)- It can range from R4000 to R200 thousand, depending on how long the body has been at the morgue.
(MacFarlane)- By the time Sethu’s family agreed to cremate her, the bill had run to R117 thousand.
(MacFarlane)- One teacher living in China told us that she’s carried the ashes of her compatriots home on multiple occasions.
(MacFarlane)- To save on courier costs, the families sign over power of attorney to the traveling teacher, she authorises the cremation and receives paperwork to take the ashes back to South Africa.
(MacFarlane)- It’s an offer Noeleen also received, but she refused.
(Noeleen Venter)- I don’t trust anyone or anything at this stage. I want his body back and I will take it from there.
(MacFarlane)- But, apparently unknowingly, she signed this form in June, authorising her son’s cremation.
(MacFarlane)- After months of trying to track down which Chinese mortuary Jarred was being kept in, the form’s instruction came to light last month.
(MacFarlane)- In a state of panic, she resubmitted the form. This time clearly stating that she wanted Jarred’s body returned to her.
(MacFarlane)- But it may be too late, says Monyela.
(Clayson Monyela)- The Chinese, duly informed by the decision of the family and which has been confirmed by the police, and continued then with process of cremation.
(MacFarlane)- However Noeleen claims she is receiving contradictory information from the very same Monyela’s office.
(Noeleen Venter)- I don’t know where the body is at this stage, once I’ve found that out then I can take it from there.
(Noeleen Venter)- DIRCO says they know what’s happening to the body but the insurance company has taken over the body.
(MacFarlane)- She shows us this email from Dirco, confirming that Jarred had indeed not yet been cremated.
(MacFarlane)- It was sent to her the same day as our interview with Monyela.
(MacFarlane)- So was Jarred cremated or not? Does Dirco know the truth? And will Noeleen ever know?
(Noeleen Venter)- I don’t know which day, which hour. I’m sure if you die, doesn’t the doctor say you died at this time or this day, I don’t know which day, which time. I don’t know how and this to me is very frustrating.
(Noeleen Venter)- If they’ve cremated him, I will never ever know how my son died. I will never know.

(Noeleen Venter)- No. He was very happy in his working environment, from what I picked up. (McFarlane)- But in June this year, Jarred’s updates suddenly stopped. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): What happens when a South African citizen dies while working abroad.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We speak to someone who has been tasked with bringing back bodies of South African teachers who die abroad, her methods, unconventional to say the least.
metadata.Summary: In August last year, 26-year-old Jarred Anthony Clegg left South Africa for China, where he would be teaching. It was an exciting time for both he and his family as teaching was his passion. Jarred had gotten hold of the opportunity through an agent that had previously sent many South African teachers to China. All was well until June this year. Four months ago, Noeleen Venter, Jarred's mom, received a call from someone who identified themselves as Jarred's friend and colleague who was also based in China. The caller told Noeleen that Jarred had died and the family needed to make arrangements to bring his body back to SA. Noeleen then contacted the agency Jarred was employed by and they confirmed his death, stating that he had died naturally in his apartment. However soon after, Noeleen received a document stating that Jarred had died in an accident and had been convicted of manslaughter. While she was processing this information, she received a document stating that Jarred had died under suspicious circumstances and the matter was now handed to the police for a criminal investigation. Lastly, she was told that her son was a victim of an accident where a vehicle had crashed into him and he died. Sitting with four official documents stating different causes of death, she reached out to a lawyer. Months later, she is desperate to get her son's ashes back but is now receicving a cold shoulder from Dirco, the Chinese Embassy as well as the agent that Jarred was employed by. All Noeleen wants is to know what happened to her son and just where are his ashes. In an effort to get more information, researchg has led us to Nadia who is a South African teacher based in China. She explained that many families find themselves in the same position as Noeleen. She says on many occassions, she has had to carry ashes of deceased South Africans in her luggage during her visits back to South Africa. She says they do this in order to cut costs of transporting the back to SA. We've also gotten hold of an agency that is based in Pretoria, they help place teachers in China and help them get their paperwork processed. The agency says they constantly have issues with DIRCO and the SA consulate in China not playing ball in cases where there are issues or even deaths of SA citizens in China.
